question: According to the manual, each traffic lane gives a motorcycle how many paths of travel to choose from?
choice_a: One
choice_b: Two
choice_c: Three
choice_d: Four
explanation: Each traffic lane gives a motorcycle three paths of travel, as indicated in the manual's lane-position illustration.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.11, 'Lane Positions'

question: Does the manual say any portion of the lane should always be avoided?
choice_a: Yes -- the center portion should always be avoided
choice_b: Yes -- the left portion should always be avoided
choice_c: Yes -- the right portion should always be avoided
choice_d: No -- no portion of the lane need be avoided, including the center
explanation: In general, there is no single best position for riders, and no portion of the lane need be avoided -- including the center. Position yourself where you are most likely to be seen and maintain a space cushion.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.11, 'Lane Positions'

question: If vehicles are being operated on both sides of you, the manual says your best lane position is usually:
choice_a: The far left edge of the lane
choice_b: The center of the lane (path 2)
choice_c: The far right edge of the lane
choice_d: As close as possible to the vehicle on your right
explanation: If vehicles are being operated on both sides of you, the center of the lane, path 2, is usually your best option.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.11, 'Lane Positions'

question: According to the manual, the oily center strip on most roads is usually no more than how wide, and unless the road is wet, provides:
choice_a: Two feet wide, with adequate traction to ride on safely
choice_b: Six feet wide, with no usable traction
choice_c: Two feet wide, with no traction at all
choice_d: It varies too much to generalize
explanation: The oily strip in the center portion is usually no more than two feet wide. Unless the road is wet, the average center strip permits adequate traction to ride on safely.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.11-12, 'Lane Positions'

question: The manual identifies 'following too closely' as:
choice_a: A minor issue compared to speeding
choice_b: Only a problem for inexperienced car drivers, not riders
choice_c: A major factor in crashes involving motorcyclists
choice_d: Not a significant crash factor for motorcycles
explanation: 'Following too closely' is a major factor in crashes involving motorcyclists. In traffic, motorcycles need as much distance to stop as cars.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.12, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: Normally, how much following distance should be maintained behind the vehicle ahead?
choice_a: A minimum of one second
choice_b: About one car length, regardless of speed
choice_c: Two seconds is always sufficient
choice_d: A minimum of four seconds
explanation: Normally, a minimum of four seconds distance should be maintained behind the vehicle ahead.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.12, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: To gauge your following distance, the manual says to pick a fixed marker on the road and begin counting seconds when:
choice_a: Your own front wheel passes the marker
choice_b: The rear bumper of the vehicle ahead passes the marker
choice_c: You first see the vehicle ahead in the distance
choice_d: The vehicle ahead brakes
explanation: Pick out a marker on or near the road ahead. When the rear bumper of the vehicle ahead passes the marker, count off the seconds. If you reach the marker before you reach 'four,' you are following too closely.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.12, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: The manual recommends opening a five-second or more following distance when:
choice_a: The pavement is slippery, you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, or traffic is heavy enough that someone may squeeze in front of you
choice_b: You are riding alone with no passenger
choice_c: The weather is clear and dry
choice_d: You are riding a motorcycle you know well
explanation: A larger cushion of space is needed if your motorcycle will take longer than normal to stop -- if the pavement is slippery, you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, or traffic is heavy and someone may squeeze in front of you, open up a five-second or more following distance.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.12, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: Why does the manual say to keep well behind the vehicle ahead even when you are stopped?
choice_a: It is required by law at every stop
choice_b: It keeps your engine from overheating
choice_c: It makes it easier to get out of the way if someone bears down on you from behind, and gives you room if the vehicle ahead backs up
choice_d: It prevents your mirrors from fogging
explanation: Keep well behind the vehicle ahead even when you are stopped -- this makes it easier to get out of the way if someone bears down on you from behind, and gives you a cushion of space if the vehicle ahead starts to back up.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.12, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: When riding behind a car, which lane position puts your image in the middle of the driver's rearview mirror, where they are most likely to see you?
choice_a: The far left portion of the lane
choice_b: The far right portion of the lane
choice_c: Riding beside the car, not behind it
choice_d: The center portion of the lane
explanation: Riding in the center portion of the lane should put your image in the middle of the rearview mirror -- where a driver is most likely to see you.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.12, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: According to the manual, what is a better way to handle a tailgater than speeding up to lose them?
choice_a: Brake suddenly to startle them into backing off
choice_b: Change lanes and let them pass, or slow down and open up extra space ahead
choice_c: Signal a turn you don't intend to make
choice_d: Match their speed exactly so the gap never changes
explanation: Speeding up to lose someone following too closely only ends up with them tailgating you at a higher speed. A better way is to get them in front of you -- change lanes and let them pass, or slow down and open up extra space ahead.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.13, 'Being Followed'

question: In the manual's passing sequence, before moving into the left lane to pass, you should ride in the left portion of your lane at a safe following distance in order to:
choice_a: Increase your line of sight and make yourself more visible
choice_b: Warm up the engine before accelerating
choice_c: Give the car ahead a chance to speed up first
choice_d: Avoid using your turn signal
explanation: Ride in the left portion of the lane at a safe following distance to increase your line of sight and make you more visible; signal and check for oncoming traffic before moving over.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.13-14, 'Passing and Being Passed'

question: Once you begin a pass, the manual says you should ride through the other vehicle's blind spot:
choice_a: As slowly as possible, to stay visible
choice_b: Only while sounding the horn continuously
choice_c: As quickly as possible
choice_d: It doesn't matter, as long as you signal
explanation: Ride through the blind spot as quickly as possible when passing.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.13, 'Passing and Being Passed'

question: The manual states that passes must be completed:
choice_a: As quickly as possible, regardless of the posted speed limit
choice_b: Only on multi-lane highways
choice_c: Only during daylight hours
choice_d: Within posted speed limits and only where permitted
explanation: Passes must be completed within posted speed limits, and only where permitted. Know your signs and road markings.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.14, 'Passing and Being Passed'

question: When you are being passed by another vehicle, the manual says you should stay:
choice_a: As close as possible to the passing vehicle
choice_b: In the center portion of your lane
choice_c: In the portion of the lane farthest from the passing vehicle
choice_d: Stopped until the vehicle has fully passed
explanation: When you are being passed from behind or by an oncoming vehicle, stay in the center portion of your lane -- riding closer to them could put you in a hazardous situation.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.14, 'Being Passed'

question: Why does the manual warn against moving into the portion of the lane farthest from a vehicle that is passing you?
choice_a: It might invite the other driver to cut back into your lane too early
choice_b: It puts you closer to oncoming traffic
choice_c: It makes your turn signal less visible
choice_d: It is illegal under Pennsylvania law
explanation: Do not move into the portion of the lane farthest from the passing vehicle. It might invite the other driver to cut back into your lane too early.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.14-15, 'Being Passed'

question: According to the manual, lane sharing between cars and motorcycles in the same lane is:
choice_a: Encouraged in heavy traffic to save space
choice_b: Required at busy intersections
choice_c: Usually prohibited, since both need a full lane to operate safely
choice_d: Only allowed for experienced riders
explanation: Cars and motorcycles need a full lane to operate safely. Lane sharing is usually prohibited.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.15, 'Lane Sharing'

question: Drivers are most tempted to squeeze into a motorcycle's lane in all of the following situations EXCEPT:
choice_a: In heavy, bumper-to-bumper traffic
choice_b: When they want to pass you
choice_c: When you are preparing to turn at an intersection
choice_d: When you are riding on an empty rural road with no other traffic
explanation: Drivers are most tempted to squeeze by a motorcycle in heavy bumper-to-bumper traffic, when they want to pass, when the rider is preparing to turn at an intersection, or when getting into an exit lane or leaving a highway -- not on an empty road.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.15, 'Lane Sharing'

question: When a driver is entering the highway from an entrance ramp, the manual advises you to:
choice_a: Speed up to pass them before they merge
choice_b: Give them plenty of room, changing lanes if one is open or adjusting speed if not
choice_c: Flash your high beam repeatedly
choice_d: Hold your lane position and speed no matter what
explanation: Drivers on an entrance ramp may not see you on the highway. Give them plenty of room -- change to another lane if one is open, or adjust speed to open up space for the merging driver if there is no room for a lane change.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.15, 'Merging Cars'

question: Why does the manual advise against riding next to cars or trucks in other lanes when you don't have to?
choice_a: You might be in their blind spot, and they also block your escape route if you need it
choice_b: It uses more fuel than riding alone
choice_c: It is illegal in every case
choice_d: It makes your headlight less visible to them
explanation: Do not ride next to cars or trucks in other lanes if you do not have to. You might be in the blind spot of a car in the next lane, and cars in the next lane also block your escape if you come upon danger in your own lane.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.15, 'Cars Alongside'
